title: When Supreme Court Justices Rode the Circuit
hook: For over a century, sitting on the Supreme Court meant months on horseback hearing ordinary cases. Some reformers want a version of that back — and the reasons are revealing.
key_points: The Judiciary Act of 1789 required justices to 'ride circuit' — traveling to hear trial and appellate cases alongside local judges.
The duty was steadily reduced through the 19th century and formally ended in 1911, leaving the Court a purely appellate body.
A vestige survives: each justice is still assigned to a circuit for emergency applications, and federal law lets judges sit by designation on other courts.
Writing at SCOTUSblog, Josh Blackman argues justices should regularly sit on the lower courts again.
Arguments for: exposure to how their doctrines actually work in trial courts, and less isolation from the wider judiciary.
Arguments against: recusal problems when a case they touched comes up on appeal, and less time for the Court's own docket.
content_html: For America's first century, being a Supreme Court justice was mostly a travel job. The Judiciary Act of 1789 required justices to ride circuit — covering long distances to hear trial and appellate cases with local judges, then reconvening in the capital for the Court's own docket. Justices complained about it constantly, Congress trimmed it repeatedly, and in 1911 the duty was abolished, leaving today's purely appellate Court.
extra_html:
Writing at SCOTUSblog, South Texas College of Law professor Josh Blackman argues the practice deserves a comeback in modern form: justices sitting by designation on the courts of appeals, seeing how their own doctrines land when a district judge has to apply them under time pressure.

The counterarguments are practical rather than constitutional. A justice who decided a case below must sit it out when it reaches the Court, so every assignment risks costing a vote later; and hours spent on someone else's docket are hours not spent on the Court's. The debate is a good window into how court reform proposals actually get judged — less on principle than on what they do to recusals, workload, and the Court's own capacity.

related.title: Supreme Court Term Limits
related.hook: U.S. Supreme Court justices serve for life — unusual among democracies. A recurring reform would swap that for fixed terms. Why the idea keeps returning, and why it's so hard to enact.

related.title: When Judges Step Aside
related.hook: A judge who might be biased is supposed to step aside. But on the U.S. Supreme Court, each justice decides that alone — and no one can overrule them.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

flashcards.back_html: The duty, imposed by the Judiciary Act of 1789, for Supreme Court justices to travel and hear cases in the lower federal courts. It formally ended in 1911.

flashcards.prompt: What is the strongest objection to justices regularly sitting on lower courts today?

choices.text: They would have to recuse themselves when those cases reach the Supreme Court
The Constitution forbids a justice from hearing any trial-level case
Lower court judges are not permitted to sit with them

flashcards.explanation_html: A justice who ruled below cannot fairly review the same case above, so each assignment costs a vote on appeal — plus time from the Court's docket.

flashcards.prompt: What trace of circuit riding still survives?
flashcards.back_html: Each justice is assigned a federal circuit for emergency applications, and federal law still allows judges to sit by designation elsewhere.
